5. No — in the standard exercism solution, we expand the definition into tokens and then process tokens left to right, expanding user words as we encounter them. So when processing [foo, 1, +], we expand foo into its current definition [10]… hmm, wait, that's also a problem: when defining `: foo foo 1 + ;`, the stored body is [foo, 1, +]. At execution, foo expands to [10] (the current definition), then 1, + → 10 1 + = 11.

But wait — in real Forth, the inner `foo` in the definition should refer to the definition that existed at compile time (the first one, [10]). Actually, the canonical solution approach: when executing a user word, expand its tokens, and if any of those tokens are user words, expand them too (recursively at execution time). This works.

And `: dup-twice dup dup ;` → dup is built-in, keep as-is → [dup, dup]. ✓

So compile-time resolution: when defining a word, each word token in the body that is a currently-defined user word gets replaced by its (already-resolved) body. Built-in words stay as tokens.

Then at execution time: token is int → push; token is a string → if user word, recursively execute its body; if built-in, execute; otherwise ValueError("undefined operation").

- `+`: pop b, pop a → push a + b. Check underflow: need 2 items.

- `drop`: need 1 → pop.
- `swap`: need 2 → swap the top two.

class StackUnderflowError(Exception):

def _tokenize(line):

def _is_number(token):
    return re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+", token) is not None
```

def _execute(tokens, stack, words):
    for token in tokens:
        if isinstance(token, int):
            stack.append(token)
        else:
            if token in words:
                _execute(words[token], stack, words)
            elif token in builtins:
                builtins[token](stack)
            else:

```
